title: The SuperActivator Mechanism: Transformers Concentrate Reliable Concept Signals in the Tail
claim: Dense activation maps for a concept are noisy and misleading, but a few extreme-activation tokens reliably indicate true presence.
layout: 7 panels in 2x4 grid; one original image, six concept heatmaps, green boxes
description: A grid of heatmap overlays on a single photo: a car side mirror reflecting a dog, with a bench in the foreground. The top-left panel shows the original image in bold. The remaining six panels are concept-specific activation maps, titled Animal, Car, Bench, Person, Motorcycle and Chair. Each map is a patch-level overlay on a faded copy of the photo. Colors run from blue (low activation) to red (high activation). A legend at lower left pairs a green square labeled SuperActivators with a blue-to-red Activation Score colorbar. Green boxes mark a few extreme-activation tokens. They cluster on the dog for Animal and on the bench slats for Bench. They are scattered for Car. Absent concepts such as Motorcycle and Chair show broad reddish regions but no green boxes. The green boxes draw the eye first.
caption: The SuperActivator Mechanism concentrates the most informative concept signals into a sparse set of in-concept activations. Heatmaps show token-level concept activation scores, with red indicating high concept alignment and blue indicating low alignment. SuperActivators are extremely high-activation tokens, marked by green boxes, that reliably distinguish true concept occurrences even when concept activation heatmaps appear to highlight absent concepts or fail to fully capture present ones. Additional image and text examples are provided in Appendix A.
abstract: Concept vectors aim to enhance model interpretability by linking learned internal representations with human-understandable semantics, but their practical utility is often limited by noisy and inconsistent activations. In this work, we discover the SuperActivator Mechanism: a transformer dynamic that amplifies concept activation gaps, concentrating the most reliable concept evidence into a small set of highly activated tokens, which we call SuperActivators. We theoretically characterize this mechanism, proving that concept-aligned attention produces two competing effects: a tail amplification effect, where gaps among already-high activations grow disproportionately fast, and an equalization effect that eventually dominates as attention concentrates on extreme tokens. We validate the predicted tail amplification empirically, finding that in-concept activation distributions develop well-separated upper tails consistently across models, image and text modalities, and concept types. Moreover, we demonstrate the practical implications of SuperActivators for concept detection and localization. First, using only high-activation tokens as concept indicators improves detection by up to 14 F1 points over competing baselines. Second, restricting detection to the extreme activation tail is not merely sufficient but essential: including activations beyond the top 5-10% of the in-concept distribution introduces noise that degrades performance. Finally, using SuperActivators as instance-specific attribution targets yields more accurate and faithful concept localization heatmaps than using global concept vectors.
